newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban claim victories in northward push.
newsitem.headline: Taleban claim victories in northward push.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia swept northward in relentless pursuit of the country's former government forces on Monday, claiming victory over key towns and a province north of the capital Kabul.
Taleban fighters said they had bottled up former defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood in his Panjsher valley stronghold following a two-pronged advance overnight from Kabul.
The Taleban now control three quarters of the country.

The militia was halted at the village of Golbahar at the mouth of the narrow gorge leading into Panjsher after a steady advance from Charikar, 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul, through to nearby Jabal os-Siraj, fighters said.

The fighters said they were awaiting orders on whether to assault the valley -- one of the few areas still under the control of the government which the Taleban ousted last week -- but that they expected to be sent into action on Monday night.
A second prong pushed north from Jabal os-Siraj, up the Salang highway that runs north from Kabul into central Asia.
The fighters in Golbahar said Taleban troops had reached the southern end of a major tunnel on the highway.

They also said that northern Uzbek militia leader Abdul Rashid Dostum had moved significant forces into the area north of the Salang tunnel, which crosses the formidable Hindu Kush mountain range, over the past few days.
Taleban sources quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said that Kapisa province to the east of Golbahar and its capital Mahmud-i-Raqi had fallen to the militia on Monday.
Mohammad Gul, deputy Taleban commander of a military barracks near Kabul, said the militia planned to seize all the territory held by the former government.
"We intend to capture all the former government areas, including the Salang tunnel and the Panjsher," he said.

However it was not immediately clear how easy it would be for the Taleban to capture the valley, held by Masood's men throughout the 1980s against several major assaults by Soviet troops backing Kabul's then-communist government.
The speed of his retreat -- from Kabul to the valley in just three days -- seemed to have dismayed the Tajik people he leads.

"We just don't know what's happening. We don't know whether Masood has a plan or is just running," said one ethnic Tajik shopkeeper in Golbahar as a jeepload of Taleban fighters swept past in a cloud of dust.
One traveller from the Panjsher valley who arrived in Kabul on Monday said he had heard that Masood was telling his people that they could no longer rely on his protection.

Gul said that there was no immediate plan to attack Dostum, a former Masood ally who split from the ousted government in 1994 and who has kept his large fighting force and small air force neutral in subsequent fighting.
Dostum holds six northern provinces.
News of the advances set nerves on edge around Mazar-i-Sharif, an important trading centre in the far north controlled by Dostum.
Officials with his well-armed Jumbish-i-Milli faction said they were ready to fight.
"We don't want to join this war," said a senior Jumbish official who declined to be named. "But if they (the Taleban) attack, we would defend ourselves."
The Taleban set up an interim ruling council vowing to turn Afghanistan into an Islamic state soon after taking Kabul.
They have begun enforcing a purist brand of Islam that has struck fear into many educated people, especially women, in the Afghan capital.
The Taleban have barred women from workplaces and told them not to leave their homes without wearing the Islamic veil.

On Sunday they also ordered all men employed in government offices and the military to grow long beards and banned any Islamic funeral service for executed former president Najibullah because it said he was a communist.
The Taleban executed Najibullah, his brother and two other aides on Friday immediately after capturing Kabul.
Witnesses said at least four women had been beaten in public for violating Islamic dress codes by Taleban fighters wielding long chains in three separate incidents on Sunday.
Aid workers said one woman was beaten opposite the Jumhuriyet hospital in Kabul as her small son watched in tears.
